Consumer goods - Ready for direct consumption - Pharmaceutical product.
Consumer goods are finished articles that reach the buyer ready for use, and medicines are one such article.

Panama canal - Atlantic ocean - Pacific ocean.
The Panama canal cuts across the isthmus of Central America and joins the Atlantic to the Pacific, saving ships the long voyage round Cape Horn.

Plain - Fertile region - Development of Agriculture.
Plains are built of river deposits and are therefore fertile and level, which is why agriculture develops on them.

Food chain - Ecosystem - Ecological balance.
The food chain is the link through which energy passes in an ecosystem, and as long as the chain is unbroken the ecological balance is kept.

Migration - Short term - Long term.
By duration migration is of two kinds: short term or temporary, such as seasonal movement for work, and long term or permanent.

True.
In a village most of the land is under crops, pasture and farm buildings, while in a town the land carries houses, shops, offices, factories, roads and open spaces. So the two land use patterns are different.

False.
Extensive commercial agriculture is carried on over very large holdings, often of several hundred hectares, worked by machinery with very few labourers. The small farm belongs to intensive subsistence agriculture.

True.
Iron and steel is made from iron ore, coal and limestone, all of which are minerals, so it is a mineral based industry and is located near their sources.

True.
Trade between two countries is bilateral trade and trade among several countries together is multilateral trade, and these are the two main forms international trade takes.

Maps today are prepared from satellite images and digital data using Geographical Information System software, which stores, analyses and displays spatial data far faster than hand drawing.

(A) Natural disasters.
A flood, drought or earthquake forces people to leave their homes, so it is a reason for migration. Internal, external and voluntary migration are TYPES of migration, not reasons for it.

(A) Temperate coniferous forests.
These forests are pure stands of softwood, the trees are tall and straight, there is little undergrowth, the wood floats easily and the winter snow helps in dragging logs, so lumbering is commercial here rather than in the mixed equatorial forest.

(B) Sugar industry.
An agro-based industry uses the produce of farming as its raw material, and the sugar industry uses sugarcane. Iron and steel, chemicals and cement are all mineral based.

(B) Television signal areas of T.V. towers.
A functional region is organised around a node and reaches as far as that node's influence reaches, which is exactly what a transmission area is. Europe, West Bengal and the Amazon basin are formal regions with fixed boundaries.

(A) Geographica.
Strabo's Geographica, written in 17 volumes, is the encyclopaedia of the geographical knowledge of his time.

(c) Mining.
Lumbering, fishing and agriculture all depend on the forests, waters and crops that belong to particular latitudes. Mining depends on the geology of the region, that is on where the mineral happens to occur, and minerals are found in every latitude. So mining is the activity not tied directly to latitude.

(c) Woollen textile industry.
Petrochemicals, iron and steel and aluminium all use minerals as raw material. Wool comes from sheep, so the woollen textile industry is an animal based, not a mineral based, industry.

(c) Political party.
A region has a location, a geographical extent and boundaries, and it is uniform in the feature by which it is defined. A political party is an organisation of people, not a characteristic of a region.

(b) Conservation of forest.
Data collection, report writing and map drawing are the working skills of a geographer. Conservation of forest is an aim or a task of management, not a skill.

(d) Population geography.
Geology, pedology and climatology study the natural environment. Population geography studies people, so it is a branch of human geography.

People settle where they can make a living. Level land, fertile soil, water, moderate climate, minerals, industry, transport and services draw people together, while mountains, deserts, dense forests and polar cold keep them away. Since these conditions are not the same anywhere on earth, population is distributed unevenly.

A literate person can take up skilled and better paid work, use new methods and know his rights, and literate parents look after health, nutrition and family size better. So literacy and the economic and social condition of a country rise and fall together, which is why the literacy rate is used as an indicator of development.

Canada has vast coniferous forests of softwood in which the trees are tall, straight and of one kind, with little undergrowth. The wood is light and floats, so logs can be moved cheaply down the many rivers, and the frozen winter surface helps in dragging them. With low population, high demand for paper and pulp and good transport, lumbering has developed there on a large scale.

In South America the Amazon forest and the Andes cover a great part of the continent, so land is difficult. Population is thin and scattered, so both labour and market are limited; capital and technology are short; transport across forest and mountain is costly; and much of the region's wealth has gone out as raw material. These together have hindered industrial growth.

Tertiary activities are those that neither take anything from nature nor manufacture goods. Some of them serve people directly, such as teaching, medicine, transport, banking and administration, and some of them move goods from producer to consumer, which is trade. Since both kinds are included, tertiary activities cover services as well as exchange.

Relief, climate, soil, water and minerals decide what activities are possible in a region at all. Level, well watered, fertile and mineral rich land allows agriculture, industry and transport to grow, while rugged, dry or barren land does not. So regional development depends on the physical setting.

Donor region: the region people move OUT of. Its population falls, it loses people of the working age group and often the men, its sex ratio and age structure become unbalanced and labour grows short.
Recipient region: the region people move IN to. Its population rises and it gains workers, but housing, water, transport and other services come under pressure and slums may grow.

Nucleated settlement: houses are built close together in a compact group, usually around a well, a temple, a crossroads or a defensive site; land between the houses is little; social contact is close; services can be provided easily.
Dispersed settlement: houses stand far apart, each on its own field; found in hills, forests and areas of extensive farming; social contact is limited; roads, water and electricity are costly to provide.

Mining: the taking out of minerals from the earth's crust; the mineral is exhaustible and cannot be replaced; the site is fixed by geology and not by latitude; it needs heavy capital, machinery and skilled labour.
Fishing: the catching of fish from seas, rivers and lakes; fish is a renewable resource if not overcaught; the grounds lie on continental shelves where warm and cold currents meet; it needs boats, nets, cold storage and skill.

Waterways: the cheapest means for heavy and bulky goods; very slow; no track has to be built, only ports; limited to coasts, rivers and canals.
Airways: the fastest means and the costliest; carries light, valuable or urgent goods and passengers; needs airports and skilled staff; can cross mountains, deserts and oceans that other means cannot.

Physical region: defined by a natural feature such as relief, climate, soil or vegetation, as in the Himalayan region or the Thar desert; its boundary is natural and changes only over a very long time.
Political region: defined by administration, as in a state, a district or a country; its boundary is drawn by people and can be changed by a decision, as when a new state is formed.

Sub-Saharan Africa, where the adult female literacy rate is only 57 per cent, the lowest of the three regions shown.

In these regions boys are sent to school before girls, and a girl is often kept at home for housework, for the care of younger children or for early marriage. Men also need literacy for paid work outside the home. So more males than females complete schooling and the adult male literacy rate is higher everywhere in the graph.

Sub-Saharan Africa is the poorest of the three regions, with few schools, long distances to them, a shortage of women teachers and widespread poverty that keeps girls at work at home. Early marriage and childbearing end schooling early. So the female literacy rate there, at 57 per cent, is the lowest, and the gap from the male rate remains wide.

The graph shows that adult female literacy is below male literacy in every one of the three regions, and that the gap is 11 points in North Africa and West Asia, 17 in South Asia and 15 in Sub-Saharan Africa. In my opinion this gap is the more serious figure, because an educated woman raises the health, nutrition and schooling of the whole family. Female literacy should therefore be raised deliberately, through free schooling for girls, women teachers and adult literacy classes, and not left to rise on its own.

North Africa and West Asia. It has both the highest male rate, 85 per cent, and the highest female rate, 74 per cent, and the smallest gap between them, so it is the most advanced of the three in social factors.

Urban settlements are classified by the chief function they perform.
Administrative towns, such as Delhi and Washington D.C.
Commercial and trading towns, such as Mumbai and New York.
Industrial towns, such as Jamshedpur and Detroit.
Transport towns, port and route towns, such as Kandla and Singapore.
Mining towns, such as Dhanbad and Kimberley.
Religious towns, such as Varanasi and Mecca.
Educational towns, such as Pune and Oxford.
Defence towns, such as Ambala and Khadakwasla.
Recreational and health towns, such as Shimla and Mahabaleshwar.
A large city usually performs many of these functions at once, so it is called multifunctional.

A foot loose industry is one that is not tied to any particular raw material, power source or market, and can therefore be set up almost anywhere.
Its raw material is light, small in quantity and easy to carry, and the finished goods are light and valuable, so transport cost hardly matters.
It uses little power and water and does not pollute much.
It depends chiefly on skilled labour, electricity and good transport, so it is often located near a city or along a highway.
Watch making, diamond cutting, electronics, computer assembly and hairpin making are examples.

Trade cannot take place without transport, because goods must physically reach the buyer.
Transport carries the surplus of one region to the region that lacks it, and so creates the market itself.
Cheap transport lowers the delivered price of goods and widens the area over which they can be sold, which is why sea transport carries the bulk of world trade.
Fast transport makes trade in perishable goods such as milk, fruit, fish and flowers possible at all.
Canals such as the Suez and the Panama, and container ships, refrigerated wagons and air cargo, have each enlarged world trade by cutting distance, time or loss.

India has tried to reduce regional imbalance through planning.
Infrastructure is provided first - roads, railways, power, irrigation and drinking water.
Public goods and services follow - schools, colleges, hospitals and primary health centres - to raise the quality of the population.
Stimulus is given to private investment through tax concessions, cheap land in industrial estates and subsidies for backward districts.
Special programmes are run for hill, tribal, drought prone and desert areas.
Employment schemes such as MGNREGA give work in the village itself.
Growth centres are developed so that development spreads outward from them.
Decentralisation through panchayati raj lets the region plan for itself.

Geography today uses new tools and has opened new fields.
Remote sensing collects data about the earth from satellites without touching it.
Geographical Information System stores, layers and analyses that data and produces maps to order.
Global Positioning System gives the exact location of any point on the earth.
Digital cartography has replaced hand drawn maps.
These have created new areas of work - disaster management, urban and regional planning, environmental impact assessment, watershed and land use planning, transport and market analysis, and defence.
Geography has therefore become an applied and employable subject, and a geographer now works with computers as much as with maps.

Economic motivation means the use of money and money's worth to make workers and capitalists work harder, so that production increases. Bonus, extra allowances, special remuneration and promotion are its forms, and the passage calls it the most important kind of motivation.

The capitalist increases production in order to earn more profit, and for that he needs the workers to work enthusiastically. So he offers incentives, because production cannot be raised by his capital alone.

Bonus is given for work completed before the deadline, and extra allowance or remuneration is given when production is above what was expected and the quality has been maintained. It is paid so that dissatisfaction does not arise among the workers and so that they continue to work enthusiastically.

A skilled worker has training or long experience, does work needing judgement and precision, is fewer in number, earns higher wages and is harder to replace. An unskilled worker does simple manual work needing no training, is available in large numbers and earns low wages. Both are needed in a secondary activity, but the skill of the first decides the quality of the product while the labour of the second decides its quantity.

Human factors are those created by people themselves, and they can pull population into a place that the physical setting alone would not favour, or drive it away from a place that the physical setting favours.
Economic activity is the strongest of them. Wherever industry, mining, trade or plantation work offers wages, people gather. The Ruhr in Germany, the Damodar valley in India and Kimberley in South Africa are crowded because of coal, iron and diamonds, although their relief and climate are not specially inviting.
Transport and communication decide whether a place can be reached and its produce sold. Population is dense along river valleys, coasts, railway lines and highways, and thin where there are no routes, as in the interior of the Amazon basin.
Urbanisation draws people continuously from villages to towns, because towns concentrate work, education, medical care and entertainment. Mumbai, Delhi, Tokyo and New York have grown in this way.
Political factors matter greatly. A settled and peaceful government, with law and order, attracts people and investment, while war, partition or persecution empties a region, as happened in Syria and in Bangladesh in 1971. Government policy can also create population, as Brazil did by building Brasilia and India did by building Chandigarh.
Social and cultural factors work in the same way. Religious centres such as Varanasi and Mecca hold large populations; so do educational centres such as Pune and Oxford.
Technology allows people to live where they otherwise could not - by irrigating deserts, as in Israel and Rajasthan, by air conditioning and by reclaiming land, as in the Netherlands.
Thus the physical setting decides where people CAN live, but the human factors decide where they actually DO live.

Intensive subsistence agriculture is the farming of very small holdings with very heavy inputs of human labour, in order to feed the farmer's own family.
It is practised in the densely populated monsoon lands of Asia - India, China, Japan, Bangladesh, Vietnam, Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines - where population presses hard on land.
Holdings are very small, often less than a hectare, and are further fragmented by inheritance, so machinery cannot be used economically.
Labour is the chief input. The family works the land with simple tools such as the plough, hoe and sickle, and every operation from sowing to harvesting is done by hand.
The land is used to its utmost. Manure, compost and fertiliser are applied heavily, irrigation from wells, tanks and canals is used wherever possible, and two or even three crops are raised from the same field in a year, so the land is rarely left fallow.
Rice is the dominant crop where rainfall is heavy, because it gives the greatest yield per hectare and can feed the most people from the least land. Wheat, millets, pulses and oilseeds are grown where rainfall is lower.
Yield per hectare is high, because of the care given, but yield per person is low, because too many people work on too little land. Most of the produce is eaten by the family and only a small surplus is sold.
The system is therefore highly productive of food and highly inefficient of labour, and it keeps the farmer poor and at the mercy of the monsoon.
